column2: In Express, what is a middleware function?

column3: A function (req, res, next) that runs during a request, before or instead of the route
column5: Correct: middleware sits in the request pipeline and either passes control on with next() or sends a response.

column3: A separate server that sits between the browser and Express
column5: That describes a proxy. Middleware is just a function inside your Express app.

column3: A database driver like mysql2 or mongoose
column5: Those talk to a database. Middleware runs on the HTTP request itself.

column3: A special kind of .ejs template
column5: Templates render HTML. Middleware is a function in the request chain.

column2: Middleware is a function (req, res, next). You already used express.json() and express.static - both are middleware.
A middleware function runs some code but never calls next() and never sends a response. What happens to the request?

column3: Express automatically moves on to the next middleware after a second
column5: There is no auto-timeout. Express waits for you to act.

column3: It hangs - the browser waits forever because nothing handed off or responded
column5: Correct: every middleware must either call next() or end the response. Do neither and the request is stuck.

column3: Express throws a 500 error immediately
column5: No error is thrown; the request simply never finishes.

column3: The route still runs because routes always run last
column5: The route only runs if an earlier middleware calls next().

column2: Each middleware must call next() (pass control on) or send a response (res.send/json/render). Otherwise the request hangs.

column3: To group related routes into their own file, then mount them with app.use('/api/tasks', router)
column5: Correct: a Router is a mini-app of routes, so server.js doesn't become one giant file.

column3: To connect Express to a database
column5: That is a driver's job (mysql2, mongoose), not the Router's.

column3: To route the server to a different port
column5: Ports are set by app.listen(port), not the Router.

column3: To redirect the browser to another website
column5: That is res.redirect(). A Router organizes your own routes.

column2: express.Router() collects related routes. Mounting at app.use('/api/tasks', router) makes the router's '/' become /api/tasks.
A router defines router.get('/:id', ...) and is mounted with app.use('/api/tasks', router). Which URL reaches that handler?

column3: GET /:id
column5: The mount prefix is part of the real URL; /:id alone is only the path inside the router.

column3: GET /api/tasks/5
column5: Correct: the mount prefix (/api/tasks) joins the router's path (/:id), so /api/tasks/5 matches with id = 5.

column3: GET /api/tasks/id
column5: id is a parameter name; the URL carries a real value like 5, not the literal word id.

column3: GET /tasks/5
column5: The mount point is /api/tasks, not /tasks.

column2: Routes inside a router are relative to where it is mounted. /api/tasks + /:id = /api/tasks/5.
How does Express know a middleware is the central error handler rather than an ordinary one?

column3: It takes four parameters: (err, req, res, next)
column5: Correct: the four-parameter signature is how Express identifies the error handler. It also goes last.

column3: It is named errorHandler
column5: The function name does not matter to Express; the number of parameters does.

column3: It is registered with app.error() instead of app.use()
column5: There is no app.error(). Error handlers are registered with app.use() and have four parameters.

column3: It is placed first, before all the routes
column5: It must be placed last, after the routes, so errors from them reach it.

column2: An error handler has four params (err, req, res, next) and is registered last with app.use(). Thrown errors and next(err) both land there.
Your validation middleware finds that a required field is missing. Which HTTP status code should the response use?

column3: 200 OK
column5: 200 means success. The request was not valid, so this is misleading.

column3: 400 Bad Request
column5: Correct: 400 tells the client its input was wrong. Return it and do not call next().

column3: 404 Not Found
column5: 404 means the resource does not exist, not that the input was invalid.

column3: 500 Internal Server Error
column5: 500 means the server broke. A bad input is the client's fault, so use 400.

column2: Invalid input is a client error: respond 400 (often with a details list) and stop before the route runs.
A user typed their name and it may contain HTML. Which EJS tag should you use to display it safely?

column3: <%= name %>
column5: Correct: <%= %> escapes HTML, so <script> is shown as text instead of running.

column3: <%- name %>
column5: <%- %> outputs raw, unescaped HTML - dangerous for anything a user typed.

column3: <% name %>
column5: <% %> runs JavaScript but prints nothing, so nothing would appear.

column3: <%# name %>
column5: <%# %> is a comment; it is never output.

column2: <%= %> escapes (safe for user input). <%- %> is raw HTML. Always escape anything a user supplied.
You set app.set('view engine', 'ejs') and call res.render('movies', data). Where does Express look for the template?

column3: In a file named movies.html in the public folder
column5: Static files are served by express.static; rendered views are .ejs files in the views folder.

column3: In views/movies.ejs
column5: Correct: with the ejs view engine, res.render('movies') loads views/movies.ejs (the views folder is set with app.set('views', ...)).

column3: In movies.js in the routes folder
column5: That would be a router, not a template. render looks for a .ejs view.

column3: It builds the HTML from the data object automatically
column5: You still write the template; render fills it with the data you pass.

column2: res.render('name') loads views/name.ejs and fills it with the data object you pass as the second argument.
With express-session, where is a logged-in user's data (like req.session.user) actually stored?

column3: On the server; the browser only holds a cookie with the session id that points to it
column5: Correct: the cookie carries an id, and the server keeps the matching session data. This is how PHP sessions work too.

column3: Entirely in the cookie, so the browser holds the username and all session data
column5: By default the cookie holds only a signed session id, not the data itself.

column3: In the URL as a query string
column5: Session ids travel in a cookie, not the URL.

column3: In the EJS template until the page is closed
column5: Templates render once per request and keep no state. The session lives on the server.

column2: The signed cookie holds a session id; req.session data lives on the server. Same model as PHP's session cookie + $_SESSION.
In the Week 2 PHP login you wrote session_destroy() to log a user out. What is the express-session equivalent in Node?

column3: res.clearSession()
column5: There is no res.clearSession() in express-session.

column3: delete req.session
column5: You don't delete the whole object; you call its destroy() method.

column3: req.session.destroy()
column5: Correct: req.session.destroy() throws the session away, matching PHP's session_destroy().

column3: app.use(session()) again
column5: That sets up the middleware; it does not end a user's session.

column2: session_start() maps to app.use(session(...)), $_SESSION to req.session, and session_destroy() to req.session.destroy().
